cities.base: Tshongdue, the one main street, five minutes below the dzong and twenty minutes from the Taktsang car park; stay here rather than up the valley so you can walk out for dinner without arranging a car.
cities.name: Paro

cities.base: Norzin Lam around the Clock Tower Square, the only stretch of Bhutan where you can leave the hotel at eight in the evening and find something open.
cities.name: Thimphu

cities.base: The Mo Chhu riverbank upstream of the dzong rather than Khuruthang town; it is 1,200 m here, ten degrees warmer than Thimphu, and the lodges face the water.
cities.name: Punakha

cities.base: Gangtey village on the northern rim, above the marsh rather than on it, so the valley opens up below you at breakfast and you are ten minutes from the goenpa.
cities.name: Phobjikha valley

cities.base: Chamkhar town in the Choekhor valley, where the temples are strung along one river road and you can actually walk between two of them.
cities.name: Bumthang

cities.base: No beds at the pass itself. It is the 3,100 m saddle on the Thimphu to Punakha road, and everyone crossing between the two valleys stops here whether they planned to or not.
cities.name: Dochula pass

places.name: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest)
places.note: The one thing everyone comes for, and it still earns it, but start at 08:00 because the cliff falls into shadow and the trail doubles in traffic after ten; bags, phones and cameras go into lockers at the entrance and the inner chapels close over the 13:00 to 14:00 break.

places.name: Ramthangkha trailhead horse stand
places.note: The horses carry you only as far as the cafeteria, never the last 300 steep steps, and they do not bring you back down, so you pay to skip the easy half of the climb and still do the hard half on foot.

places.name: Rinpung Dzong
places.note: This is a working district administration on the lower floors and a monastery above, so it shuts for the 12:00 to 13:00 lunch hour, officials use the courtyard on weekdays, and staff start moving visitors out well before five.
places.neighborhood: West bank above the Paro Chhu

places.name: National Museum of Bhutan (Ta Dzong)
places.note: The round watchtower itself is the best exhibit and the mask and thangka rooms are properly good, but the ticket counter shuts at 16:00 and the museum closes on government and local holidays, which are frequent and not published far ahead.
places.neighborhood: Ta Dzong watchtower above Rinpung Dzong

places.name: Kyichu Lhakhang
places.note: One of the seventh-century border-taming temples and the oldest thing you will stand in here, small and dark and still in daily use; go early, before the Taktsang crowd comes back down and fills it.
places.neighborhood: Lango, five minutes north of Paro town

places.name: Nyamai Zam covered bridge
places.note: The cantilever bridge under the dzong, rebuilt after a flood, and the only free thing in Paro that is actually worth stopping for; stand on the far bank at dusk when the dzong lights come on.

places.name: Chele La pass
places.note: The highest road in Bhutan and a wall of prayer flags at the top, with Jomolhari visible on a clear morning; the drive is ninety minutes each way of tight switchbacks and it is cold enough for a hat in June.

places.name: Kila Goenpa nunnery
places.note: Around seventy nuns living in cells built into the rock face, reached by forty minutes of steep downhill from the pass road, which means forty minutes back up at 3,800 m on the way out.

places.name: Drukgyel Dzong
places.note: The 1649 fortress burned in 1951 and has been rebuilt over the last decade, so you are looking at new timber on old stone; go for the Jomolhari view up the valley behind it rather than for the building.
places.neighborhood: Head of the Paro valley, 14 km north of town

places.name: Sonam Trophel Restaurant
places.note: Upstairs on the main street and the one place in Paro that cooks Bhutanese food for Bhutanese palates; ask for the pork with radish, and tell them how much chilli you actually mean.

places.name: Mountain Cafe
places.note: Espresso that works and a balcony over the street, which makes it the default breakfast on the morning after Taktsang when nobody wants to move.

places.name: Bukhari at COMO Uma Paro
places.note: A round room with glass on three sides and the best cooking in the valley, at four times the going rate; book it, and book it as your one splurge dinner rather than twice.
places.neighborhood: COMO Uma, ridge above the Paro valley

places.name: Tashichho Dzong
places.note: This is the seat of government and the summer residence of the Je Khenpo, so on weekdays tourists only get in after the civil servants leave, roughly 17:00 to 18:30; Saturday and Sunday it opens all day from about 09:00 to 17:00, and no cameras go inside.
places.neighborhood: North Thimphu, west bank of the Wang Chhu

places.name: Buddha Dordenma
places.note: A 54 m gilded bronze Buddha finished in 2015 with 125,000 smaller ones inside it; the hall is genuinely impressive and the terrace gives you the whole Thimphu valley, but it is new and it feels new.

places.name: National Memorial Chorten
places.note: Built for the third king in 1974 and circled all day by elderly Thimphu residents with prayer wheels; come before eight, when it is entirely locals and not a stop on anyone's itinerary.

places.name: Centenary Farmers' Market
places.note: The country's biggest produce market, two floors of chillies, datse cheese, dried yak and areca nut, and it only runs Thursday to Sunday with Saturday the real day; cross the cantilever footbridge for the textile stalls at Kuendeyling.
places.neighborhood: Wang Chhu riverbank below Norzin Lam

places.name: Motithang Takin Preserve
places.note: A fenced forest enclosure holding a couple of dozen takin, the national animal, which is an odd-looking beast that mostly stands still behind wire; forty minutes you will wish you had spent on the Cheri walk.

places.name: Changangkha Lhakhang
places.note: A twelfth-century fortress temple on the ridge where Thimphu parents bring newborns to be named, so you are standing in someone's family morning rather than a monument; the prayer wheel terrace looks straight down the valley.

places.name: Folk Heritage Museum
places.note: A real three-storey rammed-earth farmhouse kept as it was, with the animals downstairs and the altar room at the top, and it explains more about rural Bhutan in an hour than any dzong will; weekend hours are much shorter than weekday ones, so check before you build a Saturday around it.

places.name: National Institute for Zorig Chusum
places.note: The painting school, where students learn the thirteen traditional crafts in classrooms you walk through; it is a working school so it is shut at weekends and during the winter and summer holidays, and with no students in the rooms there is nothing to see.

places.name: Changlimithang archery ground
places.note: Teams shooting at a target 145 m away, with the losing side singing insults at the winners between shots; there is no schedule you can book, so ask your guide in the morning whether anything is on that afternoon.

places.name: Cheri Goemba
places.note: Bhutan's first monastery, founded 1620 and still a three-year retreat centre, up 500 m of switchbacks from the road bridge; the monks in long retreat are not to be disturbed, which is the point of coming.
places.neighborhood: Dodena, head of the Thimphu valley

places.name: Babesa Village Restaurant
places.note: Bhutanese set meals served on the floor of a 400-year-old farmhouse fifteen minutes south of town; book it, because they cook to the number of people expected and walk-ins get turned away.

places.name: Ambient Cafe
places.note: Where young Thimphu sits with a laptop and a flat white, which is the closest thing to ordinary city life the trip gives you; the coffee is decent and the people-watching is the reason to stay.

places.name: Punakha Dzong
places.note: The finest building in the country, on the spit where two rivers meet, and still the winter seat of the Je Khenpo and the central monk body from roughly November to May, when parts of it close to visitors entirely; it also shuts over lunch and during ceremonies, and be there before 09:30 to have the
places.neighborhood: Confluence of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu

places.name: Punakha suspension bridge
places.note: About 180 m of steel and prayer flags over the Pho Chhu, and it moves under you enough that some people stop halfway; free, ten minutes from the dzong, and busiest in the late afternoon.
places.neighborhood: Pho Chhu, upstream of the dzong

places.name: Khamsum Yulley Namgyal Chorten
places.note: A four-storey chorten built by the Queen Mother in 1999, reached by 160 m of climbing through rice terraces from the Yebesa footbridge; the internal staircase up to the roof is the payoff, and the climb is shadeless, so go before ten.

places.name: Chimi Lhakhang
places.note: The fertility temple of Drukpa Kunley, the fifteenth-century monk who taught through obscenity, which is why phalluses are painted on half the houses in this valley; the twenty-minute walk across the rice fields is better than the temple interior.

places.name: Sopsokha souvenir row
places.note: Thirty shops selling carved wooden phalluses to tour groups at the start of the Chimi path; walk past it, because the same craft sold with any conviction is in the Thimphu handicraft stalls.
places.neighborhood: Sopsokha, at the Chimi Lhakhang trailhead

places.name: Sangchhen Dorji Lhuendrup Nunnery
places.note: A nunnery and craft school on a ridge with the whole Punakha valley below it, and almost nobody stops; the drive up is ten minutes of rough track from the main road.
places.neighborhood: Nyezergang ridge above the Punakha to Wangdue road

places.name: Mo Chhu rafting put-in at Samdingkha
places.note: Ten kilometres of easy class two water finishing under Punakha Dzong, which is the best angle on the building you will get; low water from October to April, and closed when the monsoon is running.

places.name: Talo Monastery
places.note: Terraced village and monastery at 2,800 m where the present queens' family comes from, forty minutes up from the valley floor; there is nothing arranged for visitors here, which is the reason to go.
places.neighborhood: Talo village, ridge west of Punakha

places.name: Nalanda Buddhist Institute
places.note: A working monastic college founded in 1757 with around a hundred young monks debating in the courtyard in the afternoons; ask before you photograph anyone and expect a short unannounced visit rather than a tour.

places.name: Ritsha village rice terraces
places.note: Flat paths between the red rice paddies that feed this valley, ten minutes from the dzong and completely empty of other visitors; flooded and green from June, cut and gold in October.
places.neighborhood: Ritsha, east bank below the dzong

places.name: Lobesa Village Restaurant
places.note: The standard lunch stop after Chimi Lhakhang, a buffet of ema datshi, red rice and shakam paa that is honest rather than exciting; the terrace over the valley is what you are actually paying for.
places.neighborhood: Lobesa, on the Chimi Lhakhang road

places.name: Khuruthang town market
places.note: A planned concrete grid built in the 1990s to move traders out of the dzong, and it is plain, but this is where Punakha actually shops for chillies, betel and plastic buckets.
places.neighborhood: Khuruthang, the new town below the dzong

places.name: Gangtey Goenpa
places.note: A 1613 Nyingma monastery with one of the largest assembly halls in Bhutan, rebuilt board by board in the 2000s using the original joinery; the monk village around it is the reason to walk the last part rather than drive in.
places.neighborhood: Gangtey village, on the spur above the valley

places.name: Black-Necked Crane Information Centre
places.note: Run by the Royal Society for Protection of Nature, with high-power scopes trained on the roost and a live feed for when it is too cold to stand outside; the cranes are here from late October to mid February and nothing else about this room justifies the stop outside that window.
places.neighborhood: Valley floor beside the Nakay Chhu marsh

places.name: Gangtey Nature Trail
places.note: Four and a half kilometres, almost all downhill, from the wall north of the goenpa through Semchubara village and pine forest to the valley floor; arrange for the car to meet you at Khewang or you walk the whole thing back uphill.

places.name: Nakay Chhu marsh boardwalk
places.note: Raised walkway out over the dwarf bamboo marsh, which is the only way to cross it without wrecking the ground the cranes feed on; at 3,000 m in January it is genuinely, painfully cold at dawn.
places.neighborhood: Valley floor below the Crane Centre

places.name: Khewang Lhakhang
places.note: Fifteenth-century temple with three large statues of the past, present and future Buddhas, and the natural end point of the Gangtey Nature Trail; the caretaker may or may not be there to unlock it.
places.neighborhood: Eastern side of the valley floor

places.name: Kumbu Lhakhang
places.note: A meditation temple dedicated to a pre-Buddhist Bon deity, which is unusual here, with tens of thousands of small statues packed inside; short walk up from the road and almost never visited.

places.name: Kuenzang Choling Shedra
places.note: A Buddhist college of around 300 monks; your guide has to give notice before you turn up, so decide the night before or do not go at all.

places.name: Nyelung Dechenling
places.note: One of the eight residences of the Dzogchen master Longchenpa, small and off the tourist circuit; expect a blessing and a cup of butter tea rather than an exhibit.
places.neighborhood: Western side of the Phobjikha valley

places.name: Damchen Lhakhang
places.note: One of the oldest temples in the valley and the wall paintings are the reason to open the door; it is kept locked, so someone has to fetch the key from the village.

places.name: Wangmo hand-woven carpet workshop
places.note: Set up in 1992 to train young women from the valley in carpet weaving, and you can watch the looms working; prices are workshop prices and shipping home is on you.

places.name: Semchubara village
places.note: A dozen farmhouses on the slope between the goenpa and the marsh, potato fields, and dogs; this is what the valley is when you take the monastery out of it.
places.neighborhood: Mid-slope on the Gangtey Nature Trail

places.name: Hotel Dewachen dining room
places.note: There is no restaurant scene in this valley, so you eat where you sleep; Dewachen does a decent buffet with a bukhari wood stove going and windows onto the marsh, which is as good as dinner gets at 3,000 m.

places.name: Jakar Dzong
places.note: The Castle of the White Bird, district administration since 1667, with a covered stairway running down to a water supply outside the walls; as with every dzong it is an office first, so lunchtime and after five are dead.

places.name: Kurjey Lhakhang
places.note: Three temples in a row behind a wall of 108 chortens, built around the cave where Guru Rinpoche left a body print in the rock, and the first three kings are buried here; take the footbridge from here across to Tamshing rather than driving round.

places.name: Jambay Lhakhang
places.note: Said to be one of the 108 temples built by Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century, which would make it the oldest thing in Bhutan; low, dark, and small, and the naked fire dance at the Jambay Lhakhang Drup in November is the reason people time a trip around it.
places.neighborhood: Choekhor valley, 2 km north of Chamkhar

places.name: Tamshing Lhakhang
places.note: Founded by Pema Lingpa in 1501 and holding the oldest wall paintings in the country, some of them by him; pilgrims carry a 25 kg chain mail shirt he forged three times round the temple, and you are allowed to try.
places.neighborhood: East bank of the Chamkhar Chhu

places.name: Membartsho (the Burning Lake)
places.note: Not a lake but a deep green pool in a river gorge, where Pema Lingpa is said to have surfaced with a lit butter lamp and a chest of treasure; five minutes of walking, and the rough drive out is most of the time cost.
places.neighborhood: Tang valley, 30 minutes east of Chamkhar

places.name: Red Panda Brewery and the Swiss Farm dairy
places.note: An unfiltered Swiss-style wheat beer brewed here since 2006, alongside the cheese and apple juice operation Fritz Maurer started in the 1970s; the tour is short and informal, and they sometimes shut without warning.

places.name: Wangdicholing Palace
places.note: The 1857 palace where the first king was born, reopened as a museum after a long restoration; the building itself is the exhibit and there is not a great deal in the rooms.

places.name: Thangbi Lhakhang
places.note: A 1470 temple of Shamar Rinpoche's with a hell-realm mural on the entrance wall, reached by a flat forty-minute walk up the valley from Kurjey; hardly anyone comes this far north.
places.neighborhood: Upper Choekhor valley, north of Kurjey

places.name: Ogyen Choling Manor museum
places.note: A noble family's estate turned into a museum by its own descendants, with the household kept as it was and the best written explanations in Bhutan; it is two hours each way from Chamkhar on a poor road, so it eats a day.

places.name: Ura village
places.note: Cobbled lanes and clustered stone houses around a temple at 3,100 m, the most intact old village on the road east and the women still wear sheepskin shawls; an hour and a quarter of driving from Jakar over the Shertang La.
places.neighborhood: Ura valley, 3,100 m, east of Jakar

places.name: Chamkhar main street
places.note: One street of wooden shopfronts selling buckwheat noodles, yathra weaving and honey, and the rare stretch in central Bhutan where you can walk out of the hotel and go somewhere on your own.

places.name: Swiss Guest House restaurant
places.note: The old Swiss development project guest house on the hill, where the beer and the cheese are made a kilometre away and the buckwheat pancakes are the local dish done properly; small kitchen, so give them notice.

places.name: Druk Wangyal Khang Zhang chortens
places.note: 108 memorial stupas in three tiers built in 2004 for the soldiers killed in the 2003 operation against Assamese militants, with the eastern Himalaya behind them on a clear morning; by ten o'clock most days the cloud has come up and there is no range at all.

places.name: Druk Wangyal Lhakhang
places.note: Built in 2008 for the centenary of the monarchy, and the murals are the interesting part: traditional technique used to paint helicopters, monks with laptops and the fourth king in the field.

places.name: Dochula Himalaya viewing deck
places.note: The panel names the peaks along the Tibetan border including Gangkhar Puensum, the highest unclimbed mountain in the world; October to February is the only reliable season and you want to be here by 08:00.
places.neighborhood: Dochula pass, east side of the road

places.name: Druk Wangyal Cafeteria
places.note: Glass-fronted room with a wood stove and the chortens out the window, and everyone driving between Thimphu and Punakha stops here; the coffee is average and the toilets are the real reason you will be glad it exists.
places.neighborhood: Dochula pass, beside the car park

places.name: Lungchutse Monastery
places.note: Two hours up through rhododendron and old moss-hung forest from the chortens to a small monastery with a 360 degree view; you see nothing at all until the last five minutes, so a cloudy day means four hours of trees.

places.name: Trashigang Goenpa
places.note: An 1800s retreat hermitage an hour's walk below Lungchutse, with nuns and monks in long retreat; combine it with the Lungchutse climb as a loop rather than walking up for this alone.
places.neighborhood: Below the pass on the Thimphu side

places.name: Royal Botanical Park, Lamperi
places.note: 47 square kilometres of protected forest with a lake, marked trails and 46 rhododendron species that go off together in late March and April; outside that window it is a pleasant walk and nothing more.
places.neighborhood: Lamperi, 10 km down the Punakha side

places.name: Lamperi rhododendron trail
places.note: A marked loop of about three kilometres round the lake through the rhododendron collection, flat and easy; only worth planning a stop around between mid March and early May.
places.neighborhood: Inside the Royal Botanical Park, Lamperi

places.name: Hongtsho checkpost
places.note: The immigration post where your permit to travel east of Thimphu is checked and stamped, which is a real part of how travel here works rather than a sight; budget fifteen minutes and do not be the group without paperwork.
places.neighborhood: Hongtsho village, Thimphu side of the pass

places.name: Druk Wangyel Tshechu ground
places.note: The mask dance ground used once a year on 13 December, when the dances are performed by the Royal Bhutan Army rather than by monks, which makes it unlike any other tsechu; empty and unremarkable on every other day of the year.

outings.why: Six kilometres round trip and 520 m of climbing from the car park at 2,600 m to the monastery at 3,120 m, with a long stone staircase down into the gorge and back up at the end. The altitude does most of the damage, not the distance.
outings.name: the Tiger's Nest climb
outings.season: All year. January and February mornings ice the stone steps,
outings.fallback: Walk as far as the cafeteria at 2,940 m, which is where the classic face-on view of the monastery is, and turn back there.

startsFrom.name: Satsam Chorten hotels, upper Paro valley

outings.why: An hour and a half of switchbacks up to 3,988 m, the highest road in the country, then a walk out along the prayer flag ridge and down to Kila Goenpa nunnery on the cliff below. Cold and windy even in June.
outings.name: the Chele La drive
outings.season: March to November. The pass takes snow between December and
outings.fallback: Drive to the pass, walk twenty minutes along the flags, and be back in Paro for lunch.

outings.why: The 108 Druk Wangyal chortens at 3,100 m, with the eastern Himalaya behind them if the air is clear. It is the standard stop on the transfer between Thimphu and Punakha, so build it into the drive rather than making a separate trip.
outings.name: the Dochula pass drive
outings.season: All year, but the mountains only appear on clear mornings be
outings.fallback: The chortens and the Druk Wangyal Lhakhang are worth forty minutes even when the range is hidden.

outings.why: Two hours up through rhododendron and moss forest from the pass to a small monastery at about 3,600 m, with the best clear-day Himalayan view a day walk can get you here. The forest is dense enough that you see nothing at all until the top.
outings.name: Lungchutse from Dochula
outings.season: March to November. April brings the rhododendrons out.
outings.fallback: Walk forty minutes to the first ridge of prayer flags above the chortens and turn back.

outings.why: Cross the suspension bridge at Yebesa, climb 160 m through rice terraces and pine to a four-storey chorten built by the Queen Mother, then climb its internal stairs to the roof. Short, but hot and shadeless on the way up.
outings.name: the Khamsum Yulley hike
outings.season: All year. June to August is humid and the terraces are flood
outings.fallback: Cross the bridge, walk the rice terraces for half an hour and skip the climb.

outings.why: The best building in the country, on the spit where two rivers meet, plus the long suspension bridge just upstream. The dzong is live administration and a monastic residence, so the timing matters more than the walking.
outings.name: the Punakha Dzong and the Pho Chhu bridge
outings.season: All year. Jacarandas flower purple against the walls in late
outings.fallback: The bridge and the riverbank alone take an hour if the dzong is shut for a ceremony.

outings.why: Twenty minutes across rice fields from Sopsokha to the fertility temple of Drukpa Kunley, the monk who taught with obscenity. The walk is good, the souvenir row at the start is not.
outings.name: the Chimi Lhakhang walk
outings.fallback: Walk to the first ridge above the fields for the view over the valley and turn back.

outings.why: Ten kilometres of class two water from Samdingkha down to the confluence, finishing directly below Punakha Dzong. Gentle enough for people who have never rafted and dull for people who have.
outings.name: the Mo Chhu raft
outings.season: October to April, when the river is low and clear. Monsoon f
outings.fallback: Walk the riverbank path from the dzong up to the suspension bridge instead.

outings.why: Downhill from the wall north of Gangtey Goenpa through Semchubara village and pine forest to the valley floor at Khewang, about four and a half kilometres. Easy, mostly descending, and the whole marsh is in front of you the entire way.
outings.name: the Gangtey Nature Trail
outings.season: All year. The valley is at 3,000 m and freezes hard from Dec
outings.fallback: Walk the first kilometre to the top of the meadow and have the car pick you up there.

outings.why: Several hundred black-necked cranes lift off the Nakay Chhu marsh at dawn. You need to be at the Crane Centre scopes before the light, in serious cold, and the birds decide whether it happens.
outings.name: the crane roost at first light
outings.season: Late October to mid February only. Outside that window the m
outings.fallback: The Crane Centre has scopes and a live feed of the roost from indoors, which is the honest option below minus five.

outings.why: Half an hour north to the end of the Thimphu valley road, then an hour of steep switchbacks up 500 m to Bhutan's first monastery from 1620, still a strict meditation retreat. Steep from the first step, no flat warm-up.
outings.name: the Cheri Goemba climb
outings.season: All year. Icy in the shade in January.
outings.fallback: Walk the river path at Dodena below the monastery for an hour and skip the climb.

outings.why: The three oldest religious buildings in the Choekhor valley, strung two to four kilometres apart along the river, with a footbridge between Kurjey and Tamshing so part of it is on foot. Jambay dates to the seventh century and looks it.
outings.name: the Bumthang temple loop: Jambay, Kurjey and Tamshing
outings.season: All year. Bumthang gets snow in January and February.
outings.fallback: Jambay and Kurjey alone, both roadside, take two hours.

outings.why: Forty minutes of rough road east to a gorge pool where Pema Lingpa is said to have dived in holding a butter lamp and come out with it still lit. A short walk down to the rock ledges, prayer flags everywhere, and the drive is most of the da
outings.name: Membartsho in the Tang valley
outings.fallback: Wangdicholing Palace in Chamkhar is ten minutes from the hotel and takes an hour.

outings.why: Over the 3,420 m Pele La, past Chendebji chorten, down to Trongsa Dzong and up again to Bumthang. This is a full day in a car on a mountain road, and it is the reason nine days usually means choosing Phobjikha or Bumthang rather than both.
outings.name: the Pele La drive to Bumthang
outings.season: All year. Pele La can shut for a few hours after heavy snow
outings.fallback: Fly Paro to Bumthang on the domestic sector, about 35 minutes, and give the two days back to the valleys.

destination.name: Bhutan
destination.pitch: The most controlled country you can travel in, and the control is what keeps it intact: nine days buys you Paro, Thimphu, Punakha and one valley in the middle, done properly, with a guide beside you the whole way.
destination.caveat: The Sustainable Development Fee is 100 USD per person per night, charged for every night you are in the country including arrival and departure nights, on top of hotel, guide, vehicle and food, and it is not a package price you can negotiate away; a licensed Bhutanese guide is still required for dzo Put together for you just now from what I know, rather than checked against today's opening times. Worth confirming anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: Thimphu is the only town of any size and it is one long street with no traffic lights, so do not come for urban life.
because.food: Chilli and cheese, buckwheat, red rice and dried yak, cooked well in a handful of places and blandly in hotel buffets, which is where most of your meals will happen.
because.nature: Three glacial valleys in a row at 1,200 m, 2,300 m and 3,000 m, blue pine forest all the way up, and a marsh in Phobjikha that holds several hundred black-necked cranes from late October to mid February.
because.culture: The dzongs are live government and monastic buildings, not ruins, and the tsechu mask dances are religion rather than performance.
because.adventure: The Taktsang climb, the Lungchutse ridge, and gentle rafting on the Mo Chhu; real effort at altitude, but nothing technical.
because.relaxation: Hot stone baths, long silent valleys and almost no nightlife, so the evenings are genuinely quiet rather than just early.
because.exploration: Weak, and you should know it before you book: your day is agreed with a guide the night before, and unplanned detours mostly are not possible.
